Wing + gablescheme G Split levelscheme I

Massing · site visit

Split level, on the ground

One straight axis at 200°, a 25° gable stepping at the entry, bed wing and garage held high while the living end drops half a metre into the slope. Decks down the west side and across the south. Both schemes place on the same mark, so you can stand them up one after the other and compare like for like.

Brown = cut · sand = fill · grey = retaining house 19 × 38 m

Checking whether this phone can do AR…


  


  


  

    
01Set out

    
One mark serves both schemes. Let the phone walk you to it, or pace it from a boundary mark.

    

      
      

        ———
        

      

      or open the mark in Maps →
    

    
Your blue dot and its accuracy ring show on the plan below, to scale. If the ring is bigger than the house, trust the tape, not the phone.

    
    
      
  1. 1
    Walk to the mark and put something on it — a peg, a bag, a hi-vis vest. Once you are looking through the camera you need something on the ground to aim at.
    2. 
      
  2. 2
    Step back 8–10 m, ideally uphill to the east. Tap the orange bar, allow the camera, sweep slowly at the ground until it locks a surface.
    3. 
      
  3. 3
    One finger drags, two fingers twist. Drag until the orange ring-and-cross sits on your marker, then twist until the orange arrow points true north.
    4. 
      
  4. 4
    Orange on the ground, heaviest first: the floor plates with a tick at each corner, then paving and the garage slab. The ticked green line is the zone boundary.
    5. 
      
  5. 5
    The brown and sand skin is the finished ground — brown where it is cut below what you are standing on, sand where it is filled above. Grey slabs are retaining walls. It is see-through, so the set-out lines still read underneath.
    6. 
      
  6. 6
    Past 15–20 m from where you dropped it, tracking drifts. The earthworks run 60 m end to end, so expect two or three re-places to walk the lot.
    7. 
    

    

      
The AR model carries no terrain — one flat plane at natural ground under the mark (RL −3.59). Heights read true near the mark and drift as the real hill falls away. Section 04 is the correction.

      
Paving and landform are on the second tab, not in AR — ground surfaces would fight the real ones. Interiors are solid massing, so don't walk in.

Dropping the living end half a metre has changed its character: where it used to stand clear it now cuts in — 0.4 m at the centre, 0.2 m at the entry — and only reaches pile at the south-west corner. The bed wing is unchanged: 0.3 m of cut on the east wall, 2.7 m of pile at the north tip.

    
If the model looks like it is resting on the slope rather than cutting in uphill and standing clear downhill, the AR plane locked at the wrong height — drop it again.

Retaining12 panels — both sides of the lawn

    

    
Measured on a 0.6 m grid, worked ground against natural ground, over a 46 × 62 m window. The same method on both schemes, cross-checked against the full-resolution surface to within 2%. Batters are included; topsoil and basecourse are not.

    
In the model this is the translucent skin: brown where ground is removed, sand where it is built up. Standing inside a brown patch, the finished ground is below your boots by the amount you can see.

  


  

    
07Worth looking at while you're there

    


The east wall only cuts 0.3 m — is the bench really that close to level along there?east


North tip stands on 2.7 m of pile. What is under it?master


Living floor now cuts 0.4 m in at the centre. Does that read as sunk, standing in it?living


Bed deck west edge is 3.0 m above ground. Is that a deck or a bridge?bed deck


Garage is cut 2.2 m into the slope under the bed wing. Is that face rock or loess?garage


One straight 200° axis: does every room get the outlook, or only the west side?200°
